exemplars.title: Rambler: Supporting Writing With Speech via LLM-Assisted Gist Manipulation
exemplars.why: Rambler makes speech the entry point for long-form composition, then converts spoken trains of thought into keywords, summaries, and conceptual units that support higher-level revision—an unusually complete and consequential instance of voice replacing typed authoring.
exemplars.over_the_runner_up: Rambler ranks above VoiceAlign because it demonstrates a fuller end-to-end authoring experience and a more substantial redesign of work around speech, rather than adapting utterances for an existing voice interface.

exemplars.title: VoiceAlign: A Shimming Layer for Enhancing the Usability of Legacy Voice User Interface Systems
exemplars.why: VoiceAlign is the cleanest match to the structural signature: it captures natural speech, converts it into the command syntax consumed by a legacy system, and forwards the result through a transparent virtual-audio shim.
exemplars.over_the_runner_up: VoiceAlign ranks above Orality because its evidence explicitly exposes every critical conversion stage from spoken utterance to downstream command, whereas Orality leaves the speech-to-canvas transformation underspecified.

exemplars.title: Orality: A Semantic Canvas for Externalizing and Clarifying Thoughts with Speech
exemplars.why: Orality uses a dedicated speech-input widget to turn iterative spoken thought into a persistent node-link semantic canvas, showing voice as the load-bearing authoring channel rather than merely an auxiliary transcription feature.
exemplars.over_the_runner_up: Orality ranks above NaviNote because it evidences a distinctive transformation from linear speech into a structured artifact, while NaviNote establishes a broad voice command surface but does not show the internal conversion product required by the structural signature.

notes: The final selection follows the consensus top three, but Orality is adjusted from 4.65 to 4.50 because its single figure-caption quote does not explain how speech is parsed, structured, or corrected. Rambler’s evidence clearly establishes speech-first capture and generated conceptual representations, although subsequent revisions may also use manual controls; this is permitted by the definition but makes it less structurally pure than VoiceAlign. VoiceAlign’s evidence is exceptionally direct, but its claimed impact rests only on the abstract-level mechanism rather than outcomes shown here. Orality’s evidence is the weakest of the three: readers should distrust any inference about the exact speech-to-graph conversion beyond the stated input-to-canvas relationship. NaviNote was the closest excluded candidate; its accessibility impact is strong, but the supplied quote shows voice-operated functions without the internal command or instruction representation consumed downstream.
